USER: I want to make a small weather station that shows temperature, humidity and air pressure on a little screen.
ASSISTANT [documented] Good idea. For the screen I plan to use a small I2C OLED (a 128x64 pixel display that needs only 2 data wires). It can share the same two wires as the sensor. First, pick the sensor below. All three read temperature, humidity and pressure, and they differ in wiring effort and extras.

Which sensor do you want for temperature, humidity and air pressure?
  CARDS: GY-BME280 — One chip measures all three. Small, 3.3 V, I2C (2 wires for data). Trap: many cheap boards sold as BME280 are really a BMP280 with no humidity. I can show you how to check the chip ID. | AHT20 + BMP280 combo — Two chips on one board: AHT20 for temperature and humidity, BMP280 for pressure. Works at 3.3-5 V. Needs two sensor libraries in your code. | BME680 — Same three readings plus a gas (air quality) sensor. 3.3 V, I2C. More than you need for a basic station. Gas readings need extra code. Cost class is likely higher (suggestion).
  TOOLS: search_parts, search_parts, offer_choices
  (user picks "GY-BME280")
USER: GY-BME280
ASSISTANT [documented] Here is your weather station. The BME280 sensor reads temperature, humidity and pressure. A 0.96" SSD1306 OLED (128x64 pixels) shows the values. I picked that screen because it is small and cheap. I can swap it for another one if you prefer.

Wiring: both parts share the same two data wires (I2C). SDA (data) goes to D21 (GPIO 21) and SCL (clock) goes to D22 (GPIO 22). Both parts take power from 3V3 and share GND. The sensor and screen have different addresses (the sensor is 0x76 or 0x77, the screen 0x3C or 0x3D), so they won't clash. Both boards already have I2C pull-up resistors on them, so you need no extras. The checker found no errors, no warnings and no unwired pins.

Two tips:
- Many cheap "BME280" boards are really a BMP280, which has no humidity. We can check the chip ID (0x60 is a BME280, 0x58 a BMP280) once it is wired.
- For weather readings, take about one reading per minute. Reading faster makes the sensor warm up and read too high.

Nothing changes in your project until you press "Apply to my project" on the card.
  TOOLS: propose_project, highlight
  PROPOSAL: Weather station on esp32-devkitc-30: bme280-gy, ssd1306-i2c; 0 errors
  (user presses Apply)

USER: Make an alarm: when someone walks into the room, a buzzer sounds and a red LED turns on.
ASSISTANT [documented] Good plan. You need three parts: a motion sensor, a buzzer and a red LED. I picked an active buzzer. It beeps on its own when the pin goes HIGH, so you don't need to generate a tone in code. The LED part already has its 220 Ω resistor. The one real choice is the motion sensor, so please pick a card above. After that I will draw the whole circuit for you to check. Nothing changes in your project until you press "Apply to my project".

Which motion sensor (PIR = detects body heat moving) do you want?
  CARDS: HC-SR501 PIR — The common one with two dials for range and hold time. Needs 5 V (the 5V pin). Output is 3.3 V, safe for this board. Needs about a minute to settle after power-up. | AM312 mini PIR — Very small and runs on 3.3 V, so wiring is simplest. No dials to adjust. Good for a small, fixed setup (suggestion: shorter range than the HC-SR501). | RCWL-0516 radar — Uses microwaves, not heat, and can sense through thin walls or plastic. Needs 5 V. Output stays HIGH only about 2 s after motion. It can trigger falsely more easily (suggestion).
  TOOLS: search_parts, search_parts, search_parts, offer_choices
  (user picks "AM312 mini PIR")
USER: AM312 mini PIR
ASSISTANT [documented] Here is your room alarm. The checker found no errors and no warnings.

How it works: the AM312 sensor (a PIR, which senses body heat moving) sets its OUT pin HIGH when someone walks in. Your code sees that and drives the buzzer and the LED HIGH.

Wiring:
- AM312 sensor: VCC to 3V3, OUT to IO4 (GPIO 4), GND to GND.
- Active buzzer: + (long leg) to IO5 (GPIO 5), - to GND.
- Red LED with resistor: A (long leg) to IO6 (GPIO 6), K (short leg) to GND.

Why these pins: the app picked pins that are safe on this board. They avoid the strapping pins (they change how the board boots) and the USB serial pins.

Extras to buy: none. The LED part already includes its 220 Ω resistor.

Two tips:
- Library rule: a buzzer that is loud may need a transistor. A small buzzer is fine straight from the pin. If yours is quiet or draws a lot of current, tell me and I will add a driver.
- The library does not list a settle time for the AM312. Many PIRs trigger by themselves for a few seconds after power-up (suggestion), so ignore the first alarm.

Nothing changes in your project until you press "Apply to my project" on the card.
  TOOLS: propose_project, highlight
  PROPOSAL: Room motion alarm on esp32-c3-devkitm-1: am312, buzzer-active, led-resistor; 0 errors
  (user presses Apply)

USER: Beep when something gets closer than 30 cm to my desk.
ASSISTANT [documented] Good idea. I need two parts: a distance sensor and a buzzer. The buzzer is simple: I will use an active buzzer, which beeps by itself when its pin goes HIGH. The sensor is your choice, so pick one of the cards. Then I will draw the full wiring. Nothing changes in your project until you press "Apply to my project".

Which distance sensor do you want for the 30 cm alarm?
  CARDS: HC-SR04 ultrasonic — Sound-based, needs 5 V (fine on the Uno), 4 wires: TRIG and ECHO on two digital pins. Cheap and common. Wait 60 ms between readings. | VL53L0X laser (I2C) — Light-based time-of-flight, 2 wires for data (A4/A5), pull-ups on the module. Small and precise at short range, but costs more (suggestion: price class general knowledge). | Sharp GP2Y0A21 infrared — Analog output, range 10-80 cm, one analog pin. Simple wiring, but the output is not linear, so you need a threshold from testing.
  TOOLS: search_parts, search_parts, offer_choices
  (user picks "HC-SR04 ultrasonic")
USER: HC-SR04 ultrasonic
ASSISTANT [documented] Here is the plan. The HC-SR04 sends a short burst of sound and times the echo. That time tells you the distance. When the distance drops under 30 cm, the Arduino turns the buzzer on.

Wiring:
- Sensor VCC to 5V, GND to GND.
- Sensor TRIG (start-measuring pin) to D2 (GPIO 2).
- Sensor ECHO (answer pin) to D3 (GPIO 3).
- Buzzer + (long leg) to D4 (GPIO 4), buzzer - to GND.

Why it is safe: the Uno uses 5 V logic and the HC-SR04 needs 5 V, so you need no level shifter or voltage divider. The checker found no errors or warnings. You need nothing extra to buy beyond the two parts and jumper wires.

Two tips from the library:
- Wait at least 60 ms between measurements, or the sensor reads its own old echo.
- The buzzer is an active type, so HIGH means beep and you don't need tone().

A small active buzzer is fine straight from a pin. A very loud one would need a transistor.

Nothing changes in your project until you press "Apply to my project".
  TOOLS: propose_project, highlight
  PROPOSAL: Desk proximity beeper on arduino-uno-r3: hc-sr04, buzzer-active; 0 errors
  (user presses Apply)

USER: I want my plant to get water automatically when the soil is dry.
ASSISTANT [suggestion] Here is my plan. A soil moisture sensor tells the Pico how dry the soil is. When it is dry, the Pico switches a small water pump on through a MOSFET. A MOSFET is an electronic switch, because a pin on the Pico cannot power a pump directly. First, pick a sensor. Both work with the Pico's 3.3 V logic. After your pick I will propose the full wiring. Nothing changes in your project until you press "Apply to my project".

Which soil moisture sensor do you want to use?
  CARDS: Capacitive sensor — Analog output on one ADC pin. Lower voltage means wetter soil. Works at 3.3 V. Suggestion: it usually lasts longer in wet soil, because it has no bare metal probes that corrode. | Resistive sensor (YL-69) — Has an analog output (AO) and a digital output (DO) with a trimmer to set the dry/wet threshold. Power it from 3V3. Suggestion: it is cheap, but the bare probes corrode over time in wet soil.
  TOOLS: search_parts, search_parts, search_parts, offer_choices
  (user picks "Capacitive sensor")
USER: Capacitive sensor
ASSISTANT [documented] I made a proposal. It has three parts:

- **Capacitive soil sensor.** Its AOUT pin goes to GP26 (GPIO 26), an analog pin. Lower voltage means wetter soil. Power is 3V3 and GND.
- **MOSFET module (dual AOD4184).** This is the switch for the pump. I chose it over the IRF520 because the IRF520 only half turns on at 3.3 V. The AOD4184 turns on at a gate voltage of 1.5 to 2.5 V (datasheet). Its PWM input goes to GP15 (GPIO 15). HIGH means the pump is on.
- **Mini water pump (3-5 V).** It connects to the module's OUT+ and OUT-.

**Two wires the card does not draw.** The checker would not accept the module's power inputs on board pins. Add these by hand:
- Module VIN+ to VBUS (5 V from USB)
- Module VIN- to any GND pin

VBUS is 0 V when USB is not plugged in. The pump runs from this same USB supply.

**Extras to buy:**
- A small diode across the pump, for example a 1N4007. The part notes call for a flyback diode: it absorbs the voltage spike a motor makes when it switches off. Put the stripe (cathode) on the + side.
- Tubing, and a water container.

**Calibration.** Read the sensor in dry air and in a glass of water, and note both values. Scale your dry threshold between them. The reading depends on your soil and supply voltage (library gotcha).

Nothing changes in your project until you press "Apply to my project".
  TOOLS: propose_project, propose_project, get_part, highlight
  PROPOSAL: Automatic plant watering on rpi-pico: soil-moisture-capacitive, mosfet-aod4184, water-pump-5v; 0 errors
  (user presses Apply)

USER: Two buttons, two LEDs: each button turns its own LED on and off.
ASSISTANT [documented] Here is a proposal. Each button toggles its own LED: press once for on, press again for off.

Wiring (the app picked safe pins):
- Button 1: D2 (GPIO 2) and GND
- Button 2: D3 (GPIO 3) and GND
- LED 1: D4 (GPIO 4) and GND
- LED 2: D5 (GPIO 5) and GND

Why these parts:
- Push buttons: a button wired between a pin and GND needs no extra resistor. In code use INPUT_PULLUP, which turns on a resistor inside the chip. A pressed button then reads LOW.
- LEDs with a 220 Ω resistor: the resistor limits the current, so the LED and the pin are safe at 3.3 V. The long leg (anode) goes to the pin.

Buttons bounce for a few milliseconds, so one press can look like several. Debounce them in code, for example with the Bounce2 library.

Extras to buy: nothing. The checker found no errors or warnings.

Nothing changes in your project until you press "Apply to my project" on the card.
  TOOLS: search_parts, search_parts, propose_project, highlight
  PROPOSAL: Two buttons, two LEDs on teensy-41: push-button, push-button, led-resistor, led-resistor; 0 errors
  (user presses Apply)

USER: I want a thermostat that switches a small heater on below 19 °C and off above 21 °C.
ASSISTANT [suggestion] A thermostat needs two parts: a temperature sensor and a switch for the heater. The switch will be a relay. A relay is an electric switch that the board controls. Your code will turn the heater on below 19 °C and off above 21 °C. The gap between the two limits is called hysteresis. It stops the heater from clicking on and off around one value. Pick a sensor from the cards. After that I'll ask what powers your heater, because that decides which relay fits.

Which temperature sensor do you want for the thermostat?
  CARDS: AHT20 — Temperature + humidity over I2C (a 2-wire bus). Pull-ups are on the module, so wiring is just 4 wires. Address 0x38. Good, cheap choice for a room. | MCP9808 — Temperature only, high precision, over I2C. Pull-ups are on the module. Best if 19/21 °C must be accurate. Usually costs more (suggestion). | DS18B20 probe — Waterproof probe on a cable, 1-wire. Needs an extra 4.7 kΩ pull-up resistor to 3.3 V. Good if you measure water, soil or a spot away from the board. | DHT22 — Temperature + humidity on one data pin. 3-pin modules include the pull-up. Slow: one read every 2 s, which is fine for a thermostat.
  TOOLS: search_parts, search_parts, offer_choices
  (user picks "AHT20")
USER: AHT20
ASSISTANT [documented] Good choice. The AHT20 measures temperature and humidity over I2C, a 2-wire bus. Its pull-ups are already on the module, and it answers at address 0x38. It works at this board's 3.3 V logic. One more question: what powers the heater? A relay is the switch that turns the heater on and off. The right relay depends on the heater's supply, and mains needs extra safety care.

What powers your small heater?
  TOOLS: ask_user
USER: My heater is a 12 V heating pad with its own supply, so I'll go with low-voltage DC.
ASSISTANT [documented] Here is a proposal. Nothing changes in your project until you press "Apply to my project".

**What it does:** The AHT20 measures the room temperature. Your code switches the relay on below 19 °C and off above 21 °C. The gap between the two limits stops the relay from clicking on and off around one value.

**Wiring (the checker found no errors or warnings):**
- AHT20: VIN to 3V3, GND to GND, SDA to D14 (GPIO 25), SCL to D15 (GPIO 24). These are the board's default I2C pins.
- Relay: VCC to 5V, GND to GND, IN to D2 (GPIO 10). The relay coil needs 5 V, so it uses the 5V pin and not 3V3.

**The heater side is not in the library, so wire it by hand.** Keep the 12 V pad's supply separate from the board:
1. Run the + wire of the 12 V supply to the relay's COM terminal.
2. Run the relay's NO terminal (normally open, so the pad is off when the relay is idle) to the + wire of the heating pad.
3. Connect the pad's − wire straight to the − of the 12 V supply.
4. Do not connect the 12 V supply's + to any board pin. Joining the grounds is not needed, because the relay isolates the two sides.

**Things to know:**
- Many relay modules switch ON when IN is LOW. Some do not react to a 3.3 V signal. This is from the library notes. Test it first without the heater connected: you should hear a click. If the logic is inverted, flip it in the code.
- Check that the pad's current is below the relay's rating, which is printed on the relay.
- Extras to buy: wires, and the 12 V supply you already have. The checker lists no other extras.
- The relay draws about 71 mA when on (library figure). USB can supply that.

After you apply, I can run a project check, write starter code, or help you test the relay.
  TOOLS: propose_project, highlight
  PROPOSAL: Thermostat for a 12 V heating pad on nucleo-f401re: aht20, relay-1ch; 0 errors
  (user presses Apply)

USER: I want to know when to open the window: measure the CO2 in my office and show it on a display.
ASSISTANT [documented] CO2 is the right thing to measure for "when to open the window". I found three sensors in the library that measure real CO2. Pick one in the cards. After that I'll suggest a small OLED screen to show the value. You can also tell me if you'd like a different display.

Which CO2 sensor do you want? All three measure real CO2. The CCS811, SGP30 and ENS160 only estimate it, so I left them out.
  CARDS: SCD40 (easiest) — Measures CO2, temperature and humidity. Uses I2C (a 2-wire bus) at 3.3 V. Pull-up resistors are already on the board. Only 4 wires, and it shares the bus with an OLED display. | SCD30 (more accurate, bigger) — Measures CO2, temperature and humidity with an optical (NDIR) sensor. Uses I2C at 3.3 V, with no pull-ups on the board. It stretches the I2C clock, so the code must use 50 kHz or less. It costs more than the SCD40 (suggestion, not from the library). | MH-Z19B (cheap, 5 V) — Measures CO2 only. Uses UART (serial) and needs 5 V power. Its 3.3 V TX output is fine for the ESP32. It is a bit bulky and slow to warm up (suggestion).
  TOOLS: search_parts, search_parts, offer_choices
  (user picks "SCD30 (more accurate, bigger)")
USER: SCD30 (more accurate, bigger)
ASSISTANT [documented] Here is a proposal: an SCD30 CO2 sensor and a small SSD1306 OLED screen. The card shows the full wiring table. The checker found no errors and no warnings.

How it works:
- Both parts share the same two I2C wires. SDA (data) goes to IO8 (GPIO 8) and SCL (clock) goes to IO9 (GPIO 9). They have different addresses (SCD30 0x61, OLED 0x3C or 0x3D), so they don't clash.
- Both run from 3V3 and GND.
- The SCD30 has no pull-up resistors on its board. The OLED does, so the shared bus gets its pull-ups from the OLED. Pull-ups are resistors that hold the I2C lines high.
- The app also wired the SCD30's RDY pin to IO39 (GPIO 39) and its PWM pin to IO4 (GPIO 4). You don't need either for a basic monitor. You can leave them unconnected if you prefer.

Two things to know:
- The SCD30 stretches the I2C clock, so set the bus to 50 kHz or lower in the code.
- The SCD30 needs a few seconds to give a first reading. Its CO2 value is more accurate after a few minutes of running (suggestion).

Extras to buy: none. You only need jumper wires. Nothing changes in your project until you press "Apply to my project".
  TOOLS: propose_project, highlight
  PROPOSAL: Office CO2 monitor on esp32-s3-devkitc-1: scd30, ssd1306-i2c; 0 errors
  (user presses Apply)

USER: I want to turn a small servo motor with a knob.
ASSISTANT [documented] I made a proposal: a knob (10 kΩ potentiometer) that turns an SG90 micro servo. The Arduino reads the knob and moves the servo to match.

Wiring:
- Knob: VCC to 3V3, OUT (the middle pin, called the wiper) to A0 (GPIO 14), GND to GND.
- Servo: brown wire (GND) to GND, red wire (VCC) to 5V, orange wire (SIG, the signal) to D2 (GPIO 2).

Nothing changes in your project until you press "Apply to my project".

Two things to know:
1. The checker warns that the knob is a 3.3 V part on a 5 V board and suggests a level shifter. That is a suggestion from me, not a measurement. A potentiometer is only a resistor. Powered from 3V3, its output stays at or below 3.3 V, which A0 accepts safely. I think you can skip the level shifter, but please confirm that you wired the knob's VCC to 3V3 and not 5V. The checker rejected a 5V wire to the knob, so I kept 3V3. Because of this, the knob reads about 0 to 675 instead of 0 to 1023. Scale it in code.
2. A moving servo draws short current spikes. These can reset a board that runs from USB alone (library note for the SG90). One small servo usually works. If the board restarts when the servo moves, give the servo its own 5 V supply and connect its ground to the Nano's GND.

Extras to buy: nothing else, only the Nano, the knob, the servo and jumper wires. The checker lists a level shifter, but I think you don't need it.

After you apply, I can write the starter code or check the wiring again.
  TOOLS: search_parts, search_parts, propose_project, propose_project, propose_project, highlight, get_part, get_part, get_log, get_part, check_project, highlight
  PROPOSAL: Knob-controlled servo on arduino-nano: potentiometer, servo-sg90; 0 errors
  (user presses Apply)

warnings: microSD works at 5 V and may send 5 V signals into D19, which only takes 3.3 V. Use a level shifter, or a 3.3 V version of the part.
D5 (GPIO 5) is a strapping pin. Its level at reset changes how the board boots. It usually works, but if the board fails to boot or upload, move this wire first.

USER: I want to log my bike rides: save the GPS position every few seconds to a microSD card.
ASSISTANT [documented] A bike logger needs two parts: a GPS module and a microSD card module. Both are in the library and work with this ESP32 board's 3.3 V logic. The GPS module talks over a serial link (UART). The SD card module uses SPI, a faster 4-wire bus. Pick a GPS module from the cards. Then I'll draw the whole circuit.

Which GPS module do you want for the bike logger?
  CARDS: NEO-6M (GY-NEO6MV2) — Common and cheap. 3.3-5 V, 9600 baud. First fix takes 30 s or more with sky view. Basic accuracy. | NEO-M8N (GY-GPSV3-M8N) — Newer chip, usually a better fix in poor sky (suggestion, not in library). 3.3-5 V, same 4 wires as the NEO-6M. Costs more. | BN-220 — Tiny module, light and easy to fit on a bike. 3.0-5.5 V, 9600 baud, 4 wires. | ATGM336H (GPS + BeiDou) — Cheap and small, tracks two satellite systems. Has an optional PPS pin (one pulse per second), 5 wires.
  TOOLS: search_parts, search_parts, offer_choices
  (user picks "NEO-6M (GY-NEO6MV2)")
USER: NEO-6M (GY-NEO6MV2)
ASSISTANT [documented] Here is the bike logger. The card has an Apply button, and nothing changes in your project until you press "Apply to my project".

**What it does:** the NEO-6M GPS sends its position over a serial link (UART). The ESP32 reads it every few seconds and writes a line to a file on the microSD card.

**Wiring:**
- GPS: VCC to 3V3. GND to GND. GPS TX goes to RX2 (GPIO 16). GPS RX goes to TX2 (GPIO 17). The data wires cross: each TX goes to the other side's RX.
- microSD module: VCC to VIN (5 V). The library says this module has its own 3.3 V regulator and needs 5 V. GND to GND. MOSI to D23, MISO to D19, SCK to D18, CS to D5. These are the board's standard SPI pins (SPI is a fast 4-wire bus).

**Warnings:**
1. With 5 V power, the module may send 5 V on MISO into D19, and the ESP32 only takes 3.3 V. The checker suggests a 1 kΩ + 2 kΩ divider. Put 1 kΩ in series from MISO toward D19. Then put 2 kΩ from the D19 side to GND. It's a suggestion. Many modules only output 3.3 V from the card, but the library doesn't say, so use the divider to be safe.
2. D5 (GPIO 5) is a strapping pin. Its level at reset affects boot. It usually works. If the board won't boot or upload, move CS to another pin.

**Extras to buy:** one 1 kΩ and one 2 kΩ resistor. You also need a microSD card in FAT32 format (suggestion: use a card of 32 GB or less).

**Notes for the bike:** the GPS needs a clear view of the sky. The first fix takes about 30 seconds or more, and indoors it may never get one. You will also need a 5 V power bank on the USB port while riding.
  TOOLS: propose_project, propose_project, highlight, get_part, get_part
  PROPOSAL: Bike GPS logger on esp32-devkitc-30: neo-6m-gps, microsd-module; 0 errors
  (user presses Apply)

USER: A ring of colour LEDs that flashes with the music in the room.
ASSISTANT [suggestion] Nice project. I found a 16-LED WS2812 ring in the library. It is a ring of colour LEDs that you control with one data wire. Now pick the microphone, because that changes how well the ring follows the music. The MAX4466 is the one I'd suggest for beginners (a suggestion, not a measurement). After you pick, I'll draw the whole circuit. Nothing changes in your project until you press "Apply to my project".

The LED ring will be a WS2812 ring (16 LEDs). Which microphone should listen to the room?
  CARDS: MAX4466 mic amplifier — Gives a real audio signal on one analog pin (ADC). Best for loudness that follows the music smoothly. 3 wires, powered from 3V3. | KY-038 sound sensor — Cheap module with an analog pin (AO) and a digital pin (DO) that flips above a threshold you set with a screw. Simple, but less precise. | INMP441 I2S digital mic — Digital microphone with the cleanest sound, but it needs I2S code and 5 wires. Harder for a beginner (suggestion: only if you want a spectrum effect).
  TOOLS: search_parts, search_parts, search_parts, offer_choices
  (user picks "MAX4466 mic amplifier")
USER: MAX4466 mic amplifier
ASSISTANT [documented] Here is your music light ring. Nothing changes until you press "Apply to my project".

**What it does:** The microphone listens to the room. The Pico W reads how loud it is. The ring lights more LEDs, or changes colour, as the music gets louder.

**Wiring (the app picked safe pins):**
- Microphone (MAX4466): OUT goes to GP26 (GPIO 26, an analog input). VCC goes to 3V3. GND goes to GND. The MAX4466 runs on 2.4 to 5.5 V, so 3.3 V is fine.
- LED ring (WS2812): DI (data in) goes to GP15 (GPIO 15). 5V goes to VBUS (the 5 V from USB). GND goes to GND. Leave DO empty. It only passes data to a second ring.

**Extras to buy (from the library notes, the checker did not list them):**
- A 330 Ω resistor in the data wire between GP15 and DI. It protects the first LED.
- A capacitor of about 1000 µF across the ring's 5 V and GND. It smooths power spikes. Put the long leg on 5 V.

**Good to know:**
- The ring wants a 5 V data signal, but the Pico sends 3.3 V. It often works. If the LEDs flicker or stay dark, a 74AHCT125 level shifter (a small chip that raises 3.3 V signals to 5 V) makes it reliable.
- Each LED can draw about 60 mA at full white. That is the library figure for WS2812B LEDs. It is about 1 A for 16 LEDs (my sum, a suggestion). Keep the brightness low in your code so USB can supply it.

Want starter code after you apply?
  TOOLS: propose_project, highlight, get_part, get_part, get_part, get_log
  PROPOSAL: Music light ring on rpi-pico-w: max4466, ws2812-ring; 0 errors
  (user presses Apply)

USER: Add a small display to my project so I can see the readings.
ASSISTANT [documented] I found several small displays that fit. Most are I2C screens. I2C is a two-wire bus (SDA for data, SCL for clock), and your BME280 can share those same two wires. Pick one from the cards. I'll then draw the whole circuit. Nothing changes in your project until you press "Apply to my project".

Which small display do you want to show the BME280 readings?
  CARDS: SSD1306 OLED 128x64 — Most common small OLED. I2C, 3.3 V, address 0x3C or 0x3D. Shares the same two wires (SDA, SCL) as the BME280. Fits several lines of text. | SSD1306 OLED 0.91" 128x32 — Smaller and slimmer, 3.3 V, I2C address 0x3C. Room for about 2 to 4 short lines. Same wiring as the 128x64. | SH1106 OLED 1.3" 128x64 — Bigger 1.3 inch screen, I2C, 3.3 V. Some boards swap VCC and GND, so check the printed labels first. | LCD 16x2 (I2C backpack) — Classic character screen, easy to read. It needs 5 V (VIN) and its I2C lines are pulled up to 5 V, which is less safe on a 3.3 V ESP32.
  TOOLS: search_parts, search_parts, offer_choices
  (user picks "SSD1306 OLED 128x64")
USER: SSD1306 OLED 128x64
ASSISTANT [documented] Here is the plan. The BME280 measures temperature, humidity and pressure. The SSD1306 OLED (128x64 pixels) shows them.

Both parts share the same two I2C wires: SDA on D21 (GPIO 21) and SCL on D22 (GPIO 22). Each part has its own address on the bus, so they don't clash. Power is 3V3 and GND for both.

The checker found no errors, no warnings and no unwired pins. You need nothing extra to buy. Both boards already have pull-up resistors on the I2C lines, according to the library. Pull-ups hold the lines HIGH when idle.

Two things to know:
- The OLED answers at 0x3C or 0x3D (a jumper on the back sets it). The BME280 answers at 0x76 or 0x77. They don't overlap.
- A board printed "0x78" is really 0x3C.

USER: I want two BME280 sensors: one for inside and one for outside, both read by the same board.
ASSISTANT [documented] Good plan, and the library has a part for it: the GY-BME280 breakout (3.3 V, fits this board). Two things matter for two of them. 1) Both sensors have the same I2C address by default (0x76 or 0x77). I2C is a two-wire bus where each device needs its own address. Two sensors on one bus can clash. The fix is either to set one to the other address (the breakout has a solder jumper or SDO pad for that) or to put each sensor on its own pair of pins. The library part does not list an address pin, so I would lean toward two separate buses. The ESP32 can move I2C to almost any pins. That is a suggestion, and I will check it in the wiring checker. 2) I2C over long cables (more than about 1 m) is unreliable. How far away is the outside sensor?

How far is the outside sensor from the board? This decides how we wire the two sensors.
  TOOLS: search_parts, get_part, ask_user
USER: The outside one is on the balcony with about 2 m of cable, so I'd pick 1 to 3 m.
ASSISTANT [documented] Here is a proposal. Nothing changes until you press "Apply to my project".

What it does: two GY-BME280 sensors measure temperature, humidity and pressure, one indoors and one on the balcony. One ESP32 reads both.

Wiring:
- Indoor sensor: SDA on D21 (GPIO 21), SCL on D22 (GPIO 22). These are the board's default I2C pins.
- Balcony sensor: SDA on D26 (GPIO 26), SCL on D25 (GPIO 25). This is a second, separate I2C bus. The ESP32 lets you move I2C to other pins in code.
- Both sensors get power from 3V3 and GND. They are 3.3 V parts, so they fit this board.

Why two buses: both breakouts use address 0x76 or 0x77. Separate buses mean they cannot clash, and you don't need to change a solder jumper.

The checker found no errors or warnings, and no extras to buy beyond the sensors, wire and a USB cable.

Tips (general advice, so treat them as suggestions):
- 2 m is long for I2C. The sensors have on-board pull-up resistors, which help. Use a twisted pair for SDA and SCL, or shielded cable. Keep it away from power wires. If readings drop out, shorten the cable.
- Shade the balcony sensor from sun and rain, or it will read high.
- Read in forced mode about once a minute. That keeps the chip from warming itself (library gotcha).
- Many cheap "BME280" boards are really a BMP280, which has no humidity. We can check register 0xD0 later: 0x60 means BME280, 0x58 means BMP280.
  TOOLS: propose_project, highlight
  PROPOSAL: Indoor and outdoor weather station on esp32-devkitc-30: bme280-gy, bme280-gy; 0 errors

USER: A battery-powered temperature sensor for my fridge that runs for months.
ASSISTANT [suggestion] Good project. For months on a battery, the board should sleep most of the time. It should wake only every few minutes to read the temperature. A fridge also needs a sensor that can sit in the cold, and a thin cable can pass through the door seal. I put four options in the cards. Pick one and I will draw the full circuit with the extras to buy. Nothing changes in your project until you press Apply.

Which sensor fits your fridge best?
  CARDS: DS18B20 waterproof probe — Probe on a cable. It can sit inside the fridge while the board stays outside. Needs a 4.7 kΩ resistor (extra to buy). Asleep: 0.75 µA. Library: 1 mA when measuring. | TMP117 high accuracy — Small I2C board with the best accuracy of the temperature-only parts. Pull-ups are on the board. No waterproofing, so keep it dry. Needs a short I2C cable. | AHT20 temp + humidity — Small I2C board that also reads humidity. Pull-ups on the board. No waterproofing, so keep it dry. The library has no sleep current for it. | GY-BMP280 temp + pressure — Very low current: 0.1 µA asleep, 2.7 µA measuring. No humidity, and the pressure reading is not useful in a fridge. No waterproofing.

USER: DS18B20 waterproof probe
ASSISTANT [documented] I drew a fridge sensor with one part, the DS18B20 probe. The probe goes inside the fridge on its cable. The board stays outside, and the cable passes through the door seal. The cable is thin, so it should not stop the door from closing. That is my suggestion, so try it with a sheet of paper first.

Wiring: red wire (VDD) to VDD, yellow wire (DQ) to D2 (GPIO 35, chip pin P1.03), and black wire (GND) to a GND pin.

Extra to buy: one 4.7 kΩ resistor between the yellow wire (DQ) and VDD. This is called a pull-up. It holds the data line HIGH, and the sensor pulls it LOW to send data. Without it the sensor is not found.

The checker warns that VDD is only 3.0 V on this board, and the library lists the probe as 3.3 to 5 V. So 3.0 V is a little under that range, and the probe may be unreliable. I did not use the 5V pin. It comes from a boost regulator, which would drain a battery, and the board file says never to connect it to a chip pin. If the probe is not found, tell me and I will test it.

For months on a battery, the code should:
- Read once every few minutes.
- Sleep in between.
- Give the probe 750 ms for a 12-bit reading. Shorter waits can return 85 °C, the power-on value.

Cold drains batteries faster. That is general knowledge, not from the library.

Nothing changes until you press "Apply to my project".

USER: I want an RFID card reader that opens a lock on my cupboard when I hold the right card to it.
ASSISTANT [documented] Good idea. The plan: a card reader, plus a 12 V solenoid lock (an electromagnet pin that pulls back to open the cupboard). A 5 V relay module switches the lock, because an Uno pin cannot power it directly. The lock needs its own 12 V adapter. First choose a reader from the cards. Which one you can buy and which cards you already have decides it. Nothing changes in your project yet.

Which card reader do you want to use?
  CARDS: PN532 (I2C) — Works at 5 V, so no level shifter. Only 4 wires (I2C on A4/A5). Reads 13.56 MHz cards and tags. Easiest wiring on an Uno. | RC522 (SPI) — Very common 13.56 MHz reader, usually the cheapest (suggestion). It is 3.3 V only, so on this 5 V Uno it needs a level shifter on its signal lines. More wiring. | RDM6300 (125 kHz) — Simple serial reader, runs at 5 V, no level shifter. It reads 125 kHz cards only, which are a different type from 13.56 MHz cards.
  TOOLS: search_parts, search_parts, search_parts, offer_choices
  (user picks "RC522 (SPI)")
USER: RC522 (SPI)
ASSISTANT [documented] I tried two level shifters (TXS0108E and BSS138). The wiring checker rejected both. It treats the shifter's 5 V supply pin as a signal pin. It also wired the RC522 signals straight to Uno pins, which would put 5 V on a 3.3 V-only part. The library says 5 V on the RC522 can damage it. I won't give you a drawing that could damage the part. You can switch to the PN532 reader. It runs at 5 V and uses only A4 and A5 for data, so the app can draw it correctly. Or you can keep the RC522 and I'll describe the shifter wiring in text. The lock stays the same either way: a 5 V relay switches the 12 V solenoid, and you need a 12 V adapter plus a flyback diode (a small diode across the lock coil). Nothing has changed in your project yet.

The app cannot draw a level shifter between the Uno and the RC522 without errors, and drawing the RC522 straight on the Uno's 5 V pins would be unsafe. What should I do?
  TOOLS: search_parts, get_part, get_part, propose_project, propose_project, ask_user
  PROPOSAL: RFID cupboard lock on arduino-uno-r3: rc522-rfid, bss138-level-shifter, relay-1ch, solenoid-lock-12v; 1 errors
USER: Oh, I only have the RC522, so I'll keep it and have you show me the shifter wiring by hand. I don't want to fry it. Thanks!
ASSISTANT [documented] Good call. The RC522 is 3.3 V only. Here is the plan.

**1. Press "Apply to my project" for the lock side.** It draws the relay on D7 (GPIO 7) with 5V and GND, and the relay's NO contact to the lock's +. The checker found no errors. I left the RC522 out of the drawing on purpose, because the app cannot draw a shifter between the Uno and the reader.

**2. Wire the RC522 by hand with a 4-channel BSS138 level converter.** A level shifter turns 5 V signals into 3.3 V signals and back.
- Converter power: LV to 3V3, HV to 5V, GND to GND.
- D10 (GPIO 10) to HV1, then LV1 to RC522 SDA. This pin is the chip select, not I2C.
- D13 (GPIO 13) to HV2, then LV2 to RC522 SCK.
- D11 (GPIO 11) to HV3, then LV3 to RC522 MOSI.
- D9 (GPIO 9) to HV4, then LV4 to RC522 RST.
- RC522 MISO straight to D12 (GPIO 12). This line goes from the RC522 to the Uno. A 3.3 V signal should read as HIGH on a 5 V Uno. That is a suggestion from general practice, not from the library, so test it.
- RC522 3.3V to the Uno 3V3 pin. Never use 5V. RC522 GND to GND. Leave IRQ unconnected.

**3. Lock circuit.**
- 12 V adapter + to the relay's COM.
- Relay NO to the lock's + (the drawing already has this).
- Lock - to the adapter -.
- Put a diode (for example 1N4007) across the lock: stripe side to +, other side to -. It absorbs the voltage spike when the coil switches off.

**To buy:** a 12 V adapter that suits your lock's current (check the lock's label), a BSS138 4-channel level converter, one diode, jumper wires.

Many relay modules switch on when IN is LOW. The starter code needs to handle that. Nothing changes in your project until you press Apply.
  TOOLS: propose_project, highlight
  PROPOSAL: Cupboard lock (relay and solenoid) on arduino-uno-r3: relay-1ch, solenoid-lock-12v; 0 errors
  (user presses Apply)

ASSISTANT [suggestion] Good idea: a button counter is a nice first project. First I need to know which LCD you have. The I2C version has a small board on the back with 4 pins. Which 16x2 LCD do you have?
  CARDS: LCD 16x2 with I2C backpack — Only 4 wires (GND, VCC, SDA, SCL), on the Mega's D20/D21. Easiest to wire. Has a contrast knob on the back. Library says: use VIN for VCC, 5 V logic fits the Mega. | LCD 16x2 parallel (16 pins) — No backpack, so about 10 wires plus a 10 kΩ contrast potentiometer. More wiring work, but needs no I2C. Library says: 5 V part, RW tied to GND.

USER: LCD 16x2 with I2C backpack
ASSISTANT [documented] Here is a button counter. Each press adds 1, and the number shows on the LCD.

Wiring:
- LCD GND goes to GND.
- LCD VCC goes to 5V.
- LCD SDA goes to D20 (GPIO 20).
- LCD SCL goes to D21 (GPIO 21).
- Button pin 1 goes to D22 (GPIO 22).
- Button pin 2 goes to GND.

Why these parts:
- **LCD with I2C backpack:** I2C is a 2-wire data link. It needs only 4 wires, and D20/D21 are the only I2C pins on the Mega. The library lists it as a 5 V part, so it fits the Mega's 5 V signals.
- **Push button:** In code, use INPUT_PULLUP. That turns on a resistor inside the chip that holds the pin HIGH. Pressing the button connects the pin to GND, so it reads LOW. Debounce it in code, because the contacts bounce and one press can count as several.

One warning to read:
- The checker says the button is a "3.3 V part" and asks for a level shifter. I think you can ignore this. A plain button is just a switch with no chip inside. The pin only ever sees GND or the Mega's own pull-up. This is my own judgment (a suggestion), not a library fact. You do not need to buy a level shifter.

Two tips:
- The library says to power the LCD from VIN. The board file says VIN is not fed from USB. So the proposal uses 5V, which works from USB.
- If the screen is blank or shows only blocks, turn the contrast knob on the back. If nothing answers, the I2C address may be 0x3F instead of 0x27.

Extras to buy: nothing. You need a button, 4 jumper wires for the LCD, and 2 for the button.

USER: Modulo LDR + LM393
ASSISTANT [documented] Ecco il progetto "Luce notturna automatica".

**Come funziona:** il modulo LDR misura la luce. L'LDR è una fotoresistenza, cioè una resistenza che cambia valore con la luce. Quando il valore dice "buio", l'ESP32 accende il LED.

**Cablaggio proposto:**
- Sensore VCC → 3V3. La libreria dice di usare 3V3, così l'uscita AO resta nel range dell'ADC.
- Sensore GND → GND.
- Sensore AO → D34 (GPIO 34). È un pin ADC1, quindi funziona anche con il Wi-Fi acceso.
- Sensore DO → D25 (GPIO 25). Cambia livello quando la luce supera la soglia impostata con il trimmer. Per ora è facoltativo.
- LED A (gamba lunga) → D26 (GPIO 26).
- LED K (gamba corta) → GND.

Il LED ha già la resistenza da 220 Ω. Il controllo del cablaggio non ha dato errori né avvisi. Non devi comprare altro oltre ai due componenti.
